title: Remove Element
directAnswer: Remove every occurrence of `val` in-place and return `k`, the count of surviving elements; the first `k` slots of `nums` must hold those survivors (order doesn't matter). The canonical answer is a slow/fast two-pointer pass: a write pointer `k` only advances when `fast` lands on a keeper, so `nums[k++] = nums[fast]` compacts the array in one pass, O(n) time and O(1) space.

rules: Return the **count** `k`, not the array — the grader reads only `nums[0..k)`.
**Order of survivors is free** — anything past index `k` is ignored, so you may leave garbage there.
Advance the write pointer `k` **only on a keeper**; the read pointer advances every step regardless.
Writing `nums[k] = nums[fast]` when `k == fast` is a harmless self-copy — no special-case needed.
If deletions are **rare**, the swap-with-last variant minimizes writes — mention it as the optimization.
whenToUse: Delete-in-place / compact an array to the front with O(1) extra space
Return a length and ignore the tail rather than physically shrinking
Filtering a sequence where output order is irrelevant
Any 'remove all X' where you can overwrite rather than shift
antiSignals: Order of the tail matters or you must shift elements → this still works but think Remove Duplicates
You must return a brand-new array → no in-place constraint, just filter
Removing by index range, not by value → that's a splice problem
The array is sorted and you want dedupe → Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
remember.takeaway: The slow/fast write pointer is the foundational in-place array trick: one pointer reads everything, the other only commits keepers. Internalize it here and you'll instantly solve Remove Duplicates, Move Zeroes, and Sort Colors — they're all the same skeleton.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can mutate an array in-place with O(1) space using two pointers, and whether you correctly return a count while treating the tail as throwaway.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying to physically delete/shift elements (O(n²)), or returning the modified array instead of the integer k.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name the write-pointer pattern, note that survivor order is unconstrained, and offer the swap-with-last variant as a write-minimizing optimization when removals are rare.

problemStatement:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `val`, remove all occurrences of `val` in `nums` **in-place**. The order of the elements may be changed. Then return the number of elements in `nums` which are not equal to `val`.

Consider the number of elements in `nums` which are not equal to `val` to be `k` — to get accepted, you need to do the following:

- Change the array `nums` such that the first `k` elements of `nums` contain the elements which are not equal to `val`. The remaining elements of `nums` are not important.
- Return `k`.
understanding: Compact the array so all elements not equal to val sit in the first k positions, then return k. The judge only inspects nums[0..k); whatever sits at or after index k is ignored, and survivor order doesn't matter.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the relative order of the kept elements matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — the prompt says the order may be changed and only the first k slots are checked (as a multiset). That permission is exactly what enables the swap-with-last optimization.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I have to erase or zero out the tail elements?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Everything from index k onward is explicitly 'not important', so leftover values there are fine.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, length can be 0. The loop simply never runs and we return k = 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I return the array or the count?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Return the integer k. LeetCode's harness then reads nums[0..k) itself.

examples.explanation: Two elements survive (the two 2s). The first two slots hold them; the underscores are ignored.
Five elements are not 2. They occupy nums[0..5) in some order; the last three slots are don't-cares.
The only element is removed, so k = 0 and nothing in nums is checked.

diagrams.title: Which in-place removal style to use
diagrams.caption: The slow/fast pass is the default; swap-with-last wins only when very few elements get removed.

approaches.name: Slow/Fast Write Pointer (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: This is the answer they want. Phrase it as 'a write pointer that only advances on keepers' — that framing transfers directly to Move Zeroes and Remove Duplicates.
hints: You're allowed to overwrite the array and ignore everything past some index k. Could you build the answer at the front of the same array as you scan it?
Keep two indices: one that reads every element (fast), and one that marks where the next keeper should be written (k). When does k move?
k only advances when fast points at an element that is NOT val. On a keeper, do nums[k] = nums[fast] then k++. At the end, return k.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single left-to-right pass touches each element once → O(n). Two integer indices and no auxiliary structure → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
The trick is to realize the problem hands you a free scratchpad: the array itself. Because slots from index `k` onward are declared 'not important', you can build the compacted result in-place at the front while you read the original values left to right.

**The two pointers play different roles.** The `fast` pointer is a pure reader — it visits every index `0…n−1` exactly once, no exceptions. The `k` pointer is a writer that marks the boundary between 'already-committed keepers' and 'free space'. The invariant that makes the whole thing correct: at every moment, `nums[0..k)` contains exactly the non-`val` elements seen so far, in their original relative order. Each step either preserves that invariant (when `fast` hits a `val`, we skip and `k` stays put) or extends it by one (when `fast` hits a keeper, we copy it to `nums[k]` and bump `k`).

**Why overwriting never corrupts data you still need.** Since `k` only ever lags behind or equals `fast` (`k ≤ fast` always), the slot we write to, `nums[k]`, has already been read — or it *is* `nums[fast]` itself, a harmless self-copy. We can never clobber a value we haven't yet processed. That monotone `k ≤ fast` relationship is the safety guarantee, and it's worth stating out loud in an interview.

**Why this beats the naive 'delete and shift'.** The instinct from working with lists is to find each `val` and shift everything after it left by one — but each shift is `O(n)` and there can be `O(n)` of them, giving `O(n²)`. The write pointer sidesteps shifting entirely: instead of *removing* bad elements, we *collect* good ones into the front. Same result, one pass, no shifting.

**Why we return `k` and not the array.** The grader reconstructs the multiset from `nums[0..k)`, so `k` is the only contract that matters. The leftover tail is genuinely irrelevant, which is why we never bother to clear it.
approaches.insight: Reframe 'remove the bad ones' as 'collect the good ones to the front'. That inversion is the whole pattern — once you stop thinking about deletion and start thinking about a write cursor, shifting disappears and the problem collapses to one linear pass.

diagrams.title: Write pointer compacting the array
diagrams.caption: k (write) lags fast (read). On a keeper, nums[k] is overwritten and k advances.

edgeCases.behavior: Loop body never executes; return k = 0.
Every element equals val → k never advances → return 0.
No element equals val → every step writes nums[k]=nums[fast] (self-copy) → return 2.

pitfalls: Advancing k on every iteration instead of only on keepers — corrupts the count.
Returning the array instead of the integer k.
Trying to clear or shift the tail — unnecessary work that risks O(n²).

approaches.name: Swap With Last Element (Write-Minimizing)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention when removals are expected to be rare — it does fewer writes than the standard pass because keepers are never touched.
hints: Since order doesn't matter, when you hit a val you don't have to shift — what if you just drop a fresh element on top of it from the unprocessed end?
Keep a shrinking length n. When nums[i] == val, copy nums[n-1] into nums[i] and decrement n — but don't advance i yet, because the moved element is unexamined.
If nums[i] != val, advance i normally. Stop when i reaches n. The answer is the final n.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each element is examined at most a constant number of times before i passes it or n shrinks past it → O(n) time, O(1) space. Writes happen only on removals, not on keepers.
approaches.explanation:
This variant exploits the 'order doesn't matter' permission more aggressively. Instead of streaming keepers forward, it treats the array as a pool: when index `i` lands on a `val`, we don't shift anything — we just grab the element from the current last live slot, drop it into position `i`, and shrink the live region by one.

**Why we don't advance `i` after a swap.** The element we pulled from the end (`nums[n−1]`) has never been examined — it could itself be a `val`. So after the swap we must re-test the same index `i` on the next iteration. Advancing `i` here is the classic bug: it lets a `val` that was swapped in slip through uninspected.

**Why this can be cheaper than the slow/fast pass.** In the standard write-pointer approach, every keeper is copied to `nums[k]` even when `k == i` — usually those are harmless self-copies, but they're still writes in some implementations. Here, a keeper costs *zero* writes: we only write when we actually remove something. If the array has very few `val`s (say one removal in a thousand), this does ~1 write instead of ~1000. When removals dominate, the two are comparable, so this is a situational optimization, not a strict win.

**The shrinking boundary `n` is the survivor count.** Each removal decrements `n`; each keeper just nudges `i` rightward. The loop ends when `i` and `n` meet, and `n` is exactly the number of survivors — the same `k` the other method returns.
approaches.insight: When order is free and deletions are rare, fill holes from the back instead of streaming from the front. You convert an O(removals) shifting cost into O(1) per removal, and keepers cost nothing.

edgeCases.behavior: i=0,n=1: nums[0]=nums[0] self-copy, n→0, loop ends → return 0.

pitfalls: Advancing i right after a swap — the moved-in element goes unchecked and a val can survive.
Using length() in the loop bound instead of the shrinking n.
Assuming output order matches input — it generally won't; only the multiset of survivors is guaranteed.

commonMistakes: Physically removing/shifting elements, turning an O(n) problem into O(n²).
Advancing the write pointer on every iteration instead of only on keepers.
Returning the mutated array instead of the integer count k.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Shifting instead of compacting
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Erasing each val and shifting the rest left is O(n) per removal and O(n²) overall — and easy to get off-by-one. Collect keepers with a write pointer instead.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Advancing the write pointer unconditionally
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If k++ runs even when nums[fast] == val, the count is wrong and val elements leak into nums[0..k).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Advancing i after a back-swap
commonMistakesDetailed.why: In the swap-with-last variant, the element pulled from the end is unexamined; advancing i skips it and a val can survive in nums[0..k).

patternNote: Canonical Slow/Fast Write Pointer for in-place array compaction. Recognise it whenever you must filter or partition an array with O(1) extra space and the tail is throwaway. Same skeleton as Remove Duplicates, Move Zeroes, and Sort Colors.
